name: New York City English
summary: New York City English is an urban accent with a distinctive vowel system (a split short-a, a high gliding THOUGHT vowel, no cot-caught merger, three-way Mary/marry/merry), traditional r-dropping except before vowels (now declining and variable), and in working-class speech dental or stopped t, d, th. Round 2 improved the evidence: the short-a conditions now come from a Wikipedia summary of Labov, Ash and Boberg (2006) and Labov (2007), the 'on line' and indirect-question points were re-read, and a Yale Grammatical Diversity Project page was checked for embedded-question inversion. HONEST LIMIT: reliable NYC-specific grammar is very thin in everything opened (only 'on line' is solid), so this file has only 2 grammar items instead of 8-15; do not invent more (youse, 'he don't', 'Fuhgeddaboudit' are not supported by sources opened here). Intonation is also thin: the opened sources describe conversational style (cooperative overlap), not pitch contours. Primary works (Labov 1966/2006; Labov, Ash and Boberg 2006; Newman 2014) were NOT opened directly.

grammar.condition: Metro New Yorkers say 'on line' where most Americans say 'in line' (Doll 2012 via source 1). The one NYC-specific grammar/preposition item that is solid and widely recognised.
grammar.example_standard: Are you waiting in line for the tickets?
grammar.example_dialect: Are you waiting on line for the tickets?

grammar.standard: (indirect question) She asked if she could go.
grammar.dialect: She asked could she go. (inversion in an embedded question)
grammar.condition: LOW confidence for NYC. YGDP lists 'Northeast U.S. English' (not New York City specifically) among dialects with subject-auxiliary inversion in embedded questions, usually with 'ask'; cannot be combined with 'if/whether'. Source 1 mentions a 'lack of inversion in indirect questions' as a contact feature (Labov 1972), which is ambiguous, because standard English also has no inversion there. Treat as optional colour, and use on one line at most.
grammar.example_standard: I asked her if she was coming.
grammar.example_dialect: I asked her was she coming.

pronunciation.rule: Short-a split (tensing): in closed syllables /æ/ is tense [ɛə] (higher, longer, glided) before nasals /m n/, voiceless fricatives /f θ s ʃ/ and voiced stops /b d g/; it stays lax [æ] in open syllables and in many other contexts. Variable before /dʒ/ and /z/.
pronunciation.ipa: tense [ɛə] in: man, pass, gas, bad, ask, after; lax [æ] in: cat, back, happy (examples after Labov, Ash and Boberg 2006 via source 4)
pronunciation.actor_tip: Think of 'pass' / 'bad' / 'man' with a higher, longer, slightly gliding 'a' (close to 'eh-uh'), and 'cat' / 'back' with a normal short 'a'. The same-looking vowel is two sounds.
pronunciation.example: gas (tense) vs gap (lax); bad vs back; man vs map

pronunciation.rule: Short-a exceptions: function words with a simple coda are usually lax ('can' verb-aux [æ] vs 'can't' [ɛə]); learned words and loanwords are usually lax (alas, carafe); short names (Cass, Babs) lax; words with a vowel-initial suffix keep the stem vowel (mannish tense like man); 'avenue' tense; 'ask' and 'after' tense but 'aspirin' and 'asterisk' lax.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Do not tense 'can' (auxiliary) or 'and'. Tense 'can't', 'ask', 'after'. If unsure, use the plain vowel; mixing is more natural than over-tensing.

pronunciation.rule: Raised, gliding THOUGHT: the vowel of talk, thought, all is high and gliding [ɔə], so cot and caught stay distinct (no cot-caught merger).
pronunciation.ipa: /ɔ/ -> raised, glided [ɔə] in talk, thought, all (IPA approximate, via source 1)
pronunciation.actor_tip: Round the lips, raise the tongue, and let the vowel rise slightly at the end ('taw-uck'). Keep 'cot' short and open to preserve the contrast.
pronunciation.example: talk, thought, all, caught vs cot

pronunciation.rule: Mary / marry / merry: three different vowels; no merger (unlike most of the US).
Traditional r-dropping: /r/ is dropped except before vowels (older, working-class). Today's New York speech is variably rhotic, and middle-class and younger speakers mostly keep r.
pronunciation.ipa: /r/ -> zero in coda; kept before vowels
pronunciation.actor_tip: Only for older / working-class characters: 'cah', 'foah'. Keep r in 'car alarm'. Young/middle-class: keep r.

pronunciation.rule: Th-stopping and dental t, d: th pronounced as t/d (stopped), plus dentalised t and d; Newman (2014) suggests contact with immigrant languages. Working-class and older speakers.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Put the tongue tip on the back of the upper teeth and release quickly: 'three' like 'tree', 'this' like 'dis'. Only for working-class or older characters, and not on every th word.

pronunciation.rule: Coil-curl merger: almost extinct and strongly stigmatised (Labov et al. 2006 p. 260), so do not use the old 'toity-toid' stereotype for modern characters.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Keep 'oil'/'boil' and 'earl'/'girl' as distinct standard sounds.

intonation.rule: Conversation style rather than pitch: Metro New Yorkers 'stand closer, talk louder, and leave shorter pauses between exchanges' (Tannen via source 1); overlap is cooperative, signalling engagement rather than rudeness. The same source says linguists know of no single 'normal New York conversation'.
intonation.actor_tip: In a two-hander, start your line a beat early (overlap the end of the other line) and keep volume up for banter or arguments. Do not do this for every NYC character.

common_mistakes: Dropping the r in every word for every character. It is traditional, variable and declining.
Using gangster or Sopranos-style catchphrases ('fuhgeddaboudit') to signal New York. Not supported by sources; caricature.
Tensing every short-a (and also 'can', 'and'). Use the nasal / voiceless fricative / b-d-g pattern; function words stay plain.
Using the 'coil/curl' (toity-toid) stereotype for modern speakers. The source calls the merger nearly extinct and stigmatised.
Using th-stopping on every character. It is a working-class/older feature.
Adding grammar not supported by sources (double negatives, 'youse', 'he don't'). Only 'on line' is solid.
Using 'needs washed' or other Midland/Scots-Irish patterns for New York. YGDP says the Northeast strongly rejects it.
generational_notes: Source 1: coil-curl merger largely extinct, raised THOUGHT vowel declining, r-dropping decreasing, especially among young middle- and upper-middle-class speakers.
Some young people avoid these features because of working-class associations or to avoid marking ethnicity (source 1).
Older and working-class speakers keep the most traditional features (r-dropping, th-stopping, raised THOUGHT).

Search-result summaries (not opened) say younger minority New Yorkers show a nasal-only short-a system and that young white speakers are losing the complex short-a conditions (Becker and Wong 2010; Haddican et al. 2021). Treat as to-verify.
Nostalgic words (egg cream, stickball, dungarees) read as older-generation memory.
conversion_guidelines: Natural spoken film-dialogue English first. NYC flavour comes mostly from pronunciation notes, a little vocabulary and the fast, overlapping rhythm, not from grammar.
Pick the speaker profile first: older/working-class gets the most features; young/middle-class gets few or none.
Safest two sound features per monologue: three-way Mary/marry/merry and the raised THOUGHT vowel. Add the short-a split only if comfortable.
Use 'on line' where the text has a queue. Use hero, bodega, bubkes, schmuck only where the scene has food, shops or insults; one or two at most.
Th-stopping and r-dropping only for older/working-class characters.
No eye-dialect respelling ('dese', 'dem', 'foist'). Spell words in standard English; put sounds in actor notes.
No catchphrases; no grammar beyond 'on line' (optionally one embedded-question inversion, marked low confidence).
In actor notes, state which sounds were applied, and mark short-a as 'check with a native recording'.

sources.title: Ae raising / short-a systems (Wikipedia; summarises Labov, Ash and Boberg 2006 and Labov 2007)
Inversion in embedded questions, Yale Grammatical Diversity Project
Needs washed, Yale Grammatical Diversity Project

open_questions: Primary sources (Labov 1966/2006; Labov, Ash and Boberg 2006; Newman 2014; DARE) were not opened. Short-a conditions come from a Wikipedia summary; the actual NYC rule has more lexical exceptions.
Only 2 grammar items verified. 'Youse' in NYC, 'he don't', 'them' as demonstrative and other claims were searched but no usable source was found.

The Wikipedia note that NYC lacks inversion in indirect questions (Labov 1972) is ambiguous and conflicts in direction with YGDP, which lists Northeast English with inversion. Needs the original text.
Intonation: no pitch-contour description for NYC was found. Burdin's work on Jewish English intonation (rising pitch accents, macro-rhythm) concerns Ohio and was seen only in search results.
Younger minority speakers' nasal short-a system and the loss of complex short-a conditions are from search results (Becker and Wong 2010; Haddican et al. 2021); not opened.
Borough-level differences (Brooklyn, Bronx, Queens, Long Island) not checked.
Yiddish and Italian loanwords widespread in New York (schlep, nosh etc.) were not verified as NYC-specific, so they are left out.
'Mischief Night' has no citation in the opened source and is shared with nearby areas.

sub_regions.name: 뉴욕 short-a 체계의 확산
sub_regions.note: 같은 체계가 북부 뉴저지, 올버니, 신시내티, 뉴올리언스로 퍼졌다고 합니다(Labov 2007 via source 4). 북부 뉴저지에서는 동사 can이 tense가 되는 사례도 있음.

sub_regions.name: 뉴욕 방언의 기원과 접촉
sub_regions.note: d, t의 치음화와 th-stopping은 이민 언어(이탈리아어, 이디시어) 접촉에서 왔을 가능성이 제시됨(Newman 2014 via source 1). 문법적 영향은 논쟁 중이며 이번에 검증하지 못함.

confidence_detail: medium for pronunciation (short-a conditions from a summary of the Atlas); low for grammar (only 'on line' is solid) and for intonation; medium-low for vocabulary (DARE entries seen through Wikipedia).
